narratives.narrative: The sense here (101) is that the humble God saves; the type (102) is a state, and the locus (116) is internal:ib-state - lowliness is read as a settled condition of the inner being, not a passing feeling. The role (115) is characteristic: humility is treated as a genuine mark of the person. The bearer (105) is 'the humble', the afflicted people whom the psalmist counts himself among. The operation (106) is not the humble person's act but God's response to the interior: 'you save a humble people, but the haughty eyes you bring down' - a single movement that runs source (the lowly condition) -> operation (God rescues) -> target (107: humility itself) -> coupling (112: humble-saved). The target being 'humility' and the coupling 'humble-saved' bind the low interior to deliverance: the very state of lowliness is what is rescued, while the opposite interior (haughty eyes) is abased. The discovery (114) sharpens this: two interiors are set against each other, and the psalmist reads himself among the saved. Now the silences: seat (104) is 'none' - lowliness is not lodged in a named organ (heart, spirit); it is the whole person's standing, not a faculty. Manner (108) is 'none' - the text specifies no mode of the humbling. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all absent (present:false): the passage does not trace where the humility came from, does not grade its degree, adds no qualifier, names no separate downstream effect beyond the salvation already in the operation, and issues no prohibition. The absence of an effect row is telling - the saving IS the effect, folded into the operation; the passage does not moralise the humility further. Read against the inner-being lens, God is the arena the lowly interior turns toward and is met by: humility is the condition God's rescue attaches to, pride the condition his abasement attaches to.
narratives.story: In these lines the poet describes a settled lowliness of heart - not a mood but a way of being. The picture is simple and stark: God rescues people who carry themselves humbly, and he brings down those whose eyes are proud. The poet quietly places himself among the humble, the rescued ones. Nothing is said about where this lowliness comes from, how intense it is, or any organ of the body it sits in - it is just the whole person's standing before God. And there is no separate reward tacked on: the rescue itself is the whole point. Humble people are saved; proud people are humbled - two inner postures, two very different outcomes.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'the humble God leads'; type (102) is a state, locus (116) internal:ib-state, role (115) characteristic - lowliness as a real, settled inner condition. The bearer (105) is 'the humble'. The operation (106) is God's: 'he leads the humble in what is right, and teaches them his way'; the target (107) is humility itself and the coupling (112) is humble-led. The full movement runs: the lowly interior (source-condition) -> God guides and teaches (operation) -> humility as the receptive state (target) -> bound to being led (coupling). The discovery (114) names the point precisely: only the humble are teachable; lowliness is the interior God can guide, and so they are led. The silences carry weight. Seat (104) is 'none' - the teachableness is not located in a specific organ but is the person's whole posture. Manner (108) is 'none' - no mode of leading is specified. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) are all absent: the passage does not say how the person became humble, does not grade the humility, adds no qualifier, names no downstream effect beyond the leading, and forbids nothing. The absent effect is significant - the being-led is itself the whole outcome; the text does not promise humility a further payoff. In relation to the inner being, God is the arena: the lowly self is turned toward God as pupil, and God's response is to guide it. Pride, by implication, is the interior that cannot be taught.
narratives.story: Here the poet says God leads and teaches people who are humble. The point is quietly profound: it is the lowly, teachable heart that God can actually guide - a proud heart cannot be taught. Being humble here is not a passing mood but a settled way of being, and it shows itself as willingness to be led. The poem does not explain how a person becomes humble, how deep the humility runs, or promise any extra reward for it. The whole gift is simply this: the humble get to be guided by God.
narratives.variation_note: This is one of five readings of H6035:humbl (anav). Here (Ps 25:9) the humble are the TEACHABLE interior: the operation is God leading and instructing them. It differs from #2 (Ps 69:32, the humble who see and rejoice at another's rescue), #3 (Ps 76:9, the humble as the object saved in judgment), #4 (Ps 147:6, the humble lifted up), and #5 (Ps 149:4, the humble adorned/crowned). The variation is in the operation attached to the same lowly interior - here guidance, not deliverance or exaltation - showing that humility functions as the condition of receptivity to God's instruction.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'the LORD near the brokenhearted'; type (102) a state, locus (116) internal:ib-state, role (115) characteristic - the shattered heart read as a real inner condition, not merely circumstance. The bearer (105) is 'the brokenhearted'. The operation (106) is wholly God's response: 'the LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit'; the target (107) is 'brokenness' and the coupling (112) is brokenhearted-near. The process runs: the crushed interior (condition) -> God draws near and saves (operation) -> brokenness itself as target -> bound to nearness (coupling). The discovery (114) makes the striking claim explicit: the crushed interior is not abandoned but is precisely the place of God's nearness. The silences: seat (104) is 'none' - though 'heart' and 'spirit' appear in the verse, the coding locates the brokenness not in an isolated organ but as the whole inner person's condition. Manner (108) is 'none'. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) are all absent: the passage does not say what broke the heart, does not grade the crushing, adds no qualifier, names no separate effect beyond the saving, forbids nothing. The absent source is notable - the cause of the breaking is left open; what matters is God's proximity to it. On the inner-being lens, God is the arena the broken interior is met within: far from being disqualified, the shattered heart is exactly what draws God close.
narratives.story: The poet makes a surprising claim: when a person's heart is shattered and their spirit crushed, that is precisely when God is closest. Brokenness here is a real inner condition, not just bad luck, and it is not something that shuts God out - it is what draws him near to rescue. The poem does not say what caused the heartbreak or how severe it is; that is left open. What matters is the nearness itself: the crushed person is not abandoned but found. The very place we would expect God to withdraw is the place he comes closest.
narratives.variation_note: This is one of two readings of H7665:brokenheart. Here (Ps 34:18) the broken heart is the site of God's NEARNESS and saving ('the LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit'). It differs from #2 (Ps 147:3), where the broken heart is the object of God's HEALING ('he heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds'). The same shattered interior draws two responses - here proximity/rescue, there medical mending - so the variation shows brokenness as both the place God comes close and the wound he repairs.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'the meek delight in abundant peace'; unusually the type (102) is 'affect' (not merely a state) - here meekness issues in a felt interior contentment, delight. The locus (116) is internal:ib-state and role (115) characteristic. The bearer (105) is 'the meek'. The operation (106) is 'the meek shall inherit the land and delight themselves in abundant peace'; the target (107) is 'meek-peace' and the coupling (112) is meek-delight-in-peace. The movement: lowliness (condition) -> inheriting and delighting (operation) -> peace as the target state -> bound to the meek's own delight (coupling). The discovery (114) draws out the interior payoff: meekness ends not in loss but in a peace it actively delights in. This reading is distinctive within the family because it names an emotional register (delight) as the fruit of lowliness, set pointedly against the wicked who plots and gnashes his teeth (v12) - the meek's calm contentment over against the malicious interior's agitation. The silences: seat (104) 'none' - the delight is the whole person's, not an organ's; manner (108) 'none'. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent: no origin of the meekness is traced, no degree assigned, no qualifier, no downstream effect beyond the delight already stated, no prohibition. The absent effect again shows the operation is self-contained: the delighting IS the outcome. On the inner-being lens, the arena is the land/community the meek inherit, but the true weight falls inside - a settled, peace-filled joy that contrasts with the restless, teeth-gnashing interior of the wicked (directive 5: the dark movement read alongside the bright).
narratives.story: The poet promises that gentle, unassertive people will end up secure and, more than that, deeply at peace and glad. Their lowliness does not lead to being trampled and losing everything; it leads to a quiet, abundant contentment they actually enjoy. This is set against the angry, scheming person a few lines earlier who plots and grinds his teeth - restless and bitter inside. So two inner worlds are compared: the calm delight of the humble and the churning agitation of the malicious. The poem does not explain how a person becomes meek or how strong the feeling is; it simply says the reward is peace, and that peace is its own joy.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me'; the type (102) is 'affect' - here poverty is an owned inner disposition coloured by confidence. Locus (116) internal:ib-state, role (115) characteristic. The bearer (105) is 'the psalmist'. The operation (106): 'the self is poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for it; he is its help and deliverer - lowliness confident of God's attention'; the target (107) is 'confident-lowliness' and the coupling (112) is poor-but-thought-of. The process runs: the lowly self (condition) -> the Lord takes thought for it (operation, God's) -> confident-lowliness as target -> bound to being remembered (coupling). The discovery (114) states the finding: the interior holds weakness and confidence together - it owns its poverty yet rests in being remembered by God. Silences: seat (104) 'none' - the poverty is the whole self's estate, not an organ's; manner (108) 'none'. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent: no cause of the poverty traced, no grading, no qualifier, no separate effect beyond God's thought/help, no prohibition. The un-narrated effect matters: the outcome is simply being thought of - the passage does not convert the lowliness into merit. On the inner-being lens, God is the arena the poor self turns to; the striking move is that lowliness here is not despair but assurance - the 'but' pivots owned weakness into rest.
narratives.story: The poet ends by openly admitting his own poverty and need - and then adds one crucial word: 'but'. He is poor and needy, but the Lord keeps him in mind and comes to his aid. So this is weakness owned without despair; he holds his low estate and a calm confidence at the same time. The poem does not explain how he became poor or how bad it is; it simply rests in the fact that God remembers him. Lowliness here is not the end of hope - it is the very place where hope quietly settles.
narratives.variation_note: One of six readings of H6041:poor (ani). Here (Ps 40:17) poverty is held together with CONFIDENCE - 'I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me'; the target is explicitly 'confident-lowliness' and the type is 'affect'. This differs from #2 (Ps 70:5, urgent plea for haste), #3 (Ps 74:21, the poor whose rescue turns to praise), #4 (Ps 86:1, poverty as the ground of appeal), #5 (Ps 109:16, the poor pursued by the enemy), and #6 (Ps 109:22, poverty pleaded against powerful foes). The distinctive note here is the 'but' - weakness owned yet resting in being remembered - so this reading pairs lowliness with settled assurance rather than raw urgency or victimhood.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'meekness / humility (anvah)'; the type (102) is 'status', locus (116) internal:ib-state, role (115) characteristic. This reading is unusual within the family because the bearer (105) is 'the king (his cause)' - meekness is not the lowly sufferer's condition but a royal virtue the warrior-king advances. Critically, the operation (106) is 'none' and the target (107) is 'none': the passage does NOT show meekness DOING anything or acting ON anyone - it is named as one of three causes the king rides for, not narrated as a process. This is a real finding: here humility is displayed as a possessed quality/banner rather than an inner movement with an effect. The one relational link is the coupling (112), a span-pair: meekness is 'paired with truth and righteousness' - it stands in a triad ('the cause of truth and meekness and righteousness'), taking its meaning from that company. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the surprising heart of true kingship' - gentleness at the centre of majesty and military splendour. The silences are heavy and meaningful: with operation AND target both 'none', and seat (104), manner (108) 'none', plus source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent, the passage gives meekness almost no interior machinery - it is asserted as a value the king embodies, not traced as a working of the inner life. That near-total silence is itself the point: meekness functions here as an emblem of ideal rule, its force carried entirely by the noble company it keeps (truth, righteousness). On the inner-being lens, the arena is the king's public cause; the inner-being content is thin and mostly relational - humility as royal ideal rather than felt movement.
narratives.story: In this royal wedding song, gentleness appears in a surprising place - at the heart of a warrior-king's cause. As he rides out in splendour, he rides for truth, for gentleness, and for what is right, all together. Strikingly, the poem does not show this gentleness doing anything or acting on anyone; it is simply named as one of the noble things the king stands for, taking its meaning from the company it keeps. Almost nothing is said about how it works inside a person - no cause, no intensity, no result. That near-silence is the point: here humility is held up as an emblem of true kingship, gentleness woven into majesty rather than something we watch unfold.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'crushed / contrite (dakah - a broken and contrite heart)'; type (102) 'status', locus (116) internal:heart, role (115) characteristic. This reading is unusually richly furnished (it carries dimensions the other family members lack). The bearer (105) is 'the penitent'. Uniquely in this family, the SEAT (104) is present and named: 'the heart' (a span-pair) - contrition IS lodged in an organ, the heart, unlike the many readings where seat is 'none'. Also present is the SOURCE (103), a span-pair: 'such a heart God will not despise' - the source-relation ties the contrite heart to God's non-rejection. The operation (106) is 'crushed / made contrite' (inferred) - a passive breaking; the manner (108) is present and specified: 'broken and crushed' - the mode of the contrition is itself named. The coupling (112) is a span-pair: 'paired with the broken spirit' - contrition stands beside brokenness (shabar) as the twin state of the accepted heart. The discovery (114) states the finding: the crushed heart, far from being spurned, is precisely what God will not despise - brokenness as the one acceptable approach. Now the target (107) is 'none' - the contrition is not directed AT anything; it is a condition, not an act aimed outward - a meaningful silence: contrition does not target, it simply is offered. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) are absent: no numeric grading (though manner supplies the qualitative 'crushed'), no added qualifier, no separate downstream effect beyond God's non-despising, no prohibition. On the inner-being lens, the arena is God as the one who receives the sacrifice: the contrite heart is the offering, and the whole movement is that God will not despise it. Compared with the family's many 'none'-seat readings, this passage deliberately anchors humility in the heart and names its manner - contrition is the most interiorised, organ-located member of the family.
narratives.story: After his great failure, the poet discovers what God actually wants: not animal sacrifices but a heart that has been broken open. Contrition here is deep and located right in the heart - a person crushed and humbled from the inside. And the astonishing thing is that this shattered heart is exactly what God will not turn away; it is the one offering he receives. The brokenness is not aimed at anything or anyone - it is simply the true state of a person who has come undone before God. This is the family's most inward picture of lowliness: not a public posture but a heart crushed to dust, and welcomed there.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'broken / shattered (shabar - a broken spirit)'; the type (102) is 'action' - brokenness read as something done to the inner disposition, a breaking-force, not a mere static state. Role (115) characteristic. The seat (104) is present and named: 'the spirit' (span-pair) - this brokenness IS located in an organ of the inner life, the spirit; locus (116) is internal:spirit. The bearer (105) is 'the penitent'. The operation (106) is 'be broken / shattered'; the coupling (112) is a span-pair: it 'qualifies the spirit that is God's true sacrifice'. The movement: the penitent's spirit -> shattered (operation) -> the crushed spirit becomes the acceptable offering (coupling). The discovery (114): the shattering is what makes the spirit acceptable; shabar is the breaking-force on the inner disposition that God receives as sacrifice, paralleling the bones God broke in v8. The silences: target (107) is 'none' - the breaking is not aimed at an external object; it terminates in the spirit itself. Manner (108) 'none' - unlike the contrite reading, no mode is separately named here. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) absent: no agent of the breaking is fixed in this row (though v8 implies God), no grading, no qualifier, no separate effect beyond becoming the sacrifice, no prohibition. On the inner-being lens, God is the arena that receives: the shattered spirit is offered up, and the finding (directive 6, uncomfortable but supported) is that God's true sacrifice is a broken interior, not an intact one.
narratives.story: The poet says the sacrifice God really wants is a broken spirit. Brokenness here is something that happens to the inner person - a shattering, not a calm state - and it lands specifically on the spirit. Astonishingly, this crushed spirit is not rejected; it is exactly what God accepts as an offering, more than any ritual gift. The breaking is not aimed at anyone else; it simply ends in the person's own spirit being undone. What we might think disqualifies a person is the very thing God receives.
narratives.variation_note: Two readings of H7665:broken sit at the same verse (Ps 51:17). This one (#1) reads the brokenness of the SPIRIT ('the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit'); its seat (104) is 'the spirit' and locus (116) internal:spirit. Reading #2 reads the brokenness of the HEART ('a broken and contrite heart'); its seat is 'the heart', locus internal:heart. The distinction is not decorative: the verse names two inner sites of the same shattering - spirit and heart - and the coding preserves both as separate readings. #1's coupling qualifies 'the spirit that is God's true sacrifice'; #2's coupling pairs the breaking with 'contrite' as the accepted heart's state.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'broken (shabar - a broken and contrite heart)'; type (102) 'action' - a breaking done to the interior; role (115) characteristic. The seat (104) is present: 'the heart' (span-pair); locus (116) internal:heart. The bearer (105) is 'the penitent'. The operation (106) is 'be broken'; the coupling (112) is a span-pair: 'paired with contrite as the state of the accepted heart' - here brokenness stands twinned with contrition (dakah) as the one condition God will not spurn. The movement: the penitent's heart -> broken (operation) -> joined to contrition as the accepted state (coupling). The discovery (114): the breaking that, with contrition, God will not despise - the shattered heart, twinned with the crushed, is the one approach the holy God receives. Silences: target (107) 'none' - the breaking terminates in the heart, aimed at no external object; manner (108) 'none'. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) absent: no agent of breaking fixed here, no grading, no qualifier, no separate effect beyond acceptance, no prohibition. On the inner-being lens, God is the arena of reception: a heart broken and contrite is precisely what he will not despise. Held beside #1 (the broken spirit), this reading shows the same shattering distributed across two named inner sites, heart and spirit - the passage insists brokenness reaches the whole interior.
narratives.story: The poet says God will not despise a broken and humbled heart. Brokenness here is something that has happened to the heart itself - a shattering, paired with genuine contrition. Together, broken and contrite, this is the one condition God welcomes rather than turns away. The breaking is not directed at anyone else; it simply reaches all the way into the person's own heart. Right alongside the earlier picture of a broken spirit, the poem insists the whole inner person is undone - and that undone heart is exactly what God receives.
narratives.variation_note: Two readings of H7665:broken sit at Ps 51:17. This one (#2) reads the brokenness of the HEART ('a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise'); its seat (104) is 'the heart', locus (116) internal:heart. Reading #1 reads the brokenness of the SPIRIT ('a broken spirit'); seat 'the spirit', locus internal:spirit. The difference is the inner site - heart vs spirit - and the coupling: #2 pairs the breaking with 'contrite' as the accepted heart's state, whereas #1 qualifies the spirit that is God's true sacrifice. Preserving both keeps the verse's doubled anatomy of brokenness (spirit and heart) intact.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'humble / afflicted (anav)'; type (102) 'status', role (115) characteristic. Notably the locus (116) is external:person - the humble are viewed as an external company (the God-seekers) rather than as the speaker's internal state, distinguishing this from the family's many internal:ib-state readings. The bearer (105) is 'the humble'. The operation (106) is 'see and be glad' (a span-event) - here the lowly are active subjects: they watch and rejoice. The coupling (112, span-pair) binds this to 'their gladness and the seekers' reviving' - the humble's sight of rescue issues in gladness and revived hearts. The movement: the afflicted community (bearer) -> see God's deliverance of the sufferer (operation) -> gladness/reviving (coupling). The discovery (114): the lowly are encouraged by the sufferer's deliverance; the psalmist's testimony revives the hearts of the God-seekers. Silences: seat (104) 'none'; target (107) 'none' - the gladness is not aimed at an object, it simply arises; manner (108) 'none'. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) absent: no origin of their humility, no grading, no qualifier, no separately-named effect beyond the gladness/reviving already coupled, no prohibition. On the inner-being lens, the arena is the community watching God act: humility functions socially here - one person's rescue lifts the whole lowly company. This is the family's clearest instance of humility as shared, encouraging affect rather than solitary condition.
narratives.story: When the poet is rescued, he says the humble will see it and be glad. Here the lowly are not a single suffering person but a whole watching community of people who seek God. Seeing God come through for one of their own lifts them - their hearts revive. The gladness is not aimed at anything; it simply wells up at the sight of deliverance. This shows humility as something shared and contagious: one person's rescue becomes hope for all the lowly who are watching.
narratives.variation_note: One of five readings of H6035:humbl (anav). Here (Ps 69:32) the humble are OBSERVERS who take heart at another's rescue ('when the humble see it they will be glad'); the operation is 'see and be glad' and the locus (116) is external:person - the humble as a watching community, not the psalmist's own inner state. This differs from #1 (Ps 25:9, the humble led/taught), #3 (Ps 76:9, the humble saved in judgment), #4 (Ps 147:6, lifted up), #5 (Ps 149:4, adorned). The distinctive move: humility here is contagious encouragement - the lowly are revived by seeing God rescue one of their own.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'needy / poor (ebyon - the LORD hears the needy)'; type (102) 'status', role (115) characteristic; locus (116) external:god - the reading is oriented toward God as the arena who hears. The bearer (105) is 'the needy / God's afflicted people'. A SOURCE (103) is present here (a span-pair, unusual for this family): the needy are those 'whom the LORD hears and does not despise' - the source-relation ties their neediness to God's attentive non-rejection. The operation (106) is 'heard by God' (span-event) - God's act, not theirs. The manner (108) is present and specified: 'not despised, though prisoners' - the mode of God's hearing is that it does not scorn even the imprisoned. The discovery (114): the poor and imprisoned whom God attends; the destitute assured that God hears them and never scorns his captive people. Silences: seat (104) 'none'; target (107) 'none' - the being-heard has no further object; coupling (112) is 'none' here (present but valued 'none') - the neediness is not paired with another state in this row. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113), and source-of-affliction beyond the God-relation are absent: no grading, no qualifier, no separate downstream effect beyond God's hearing, no prohibition. The 'none' coupling is itself evidence - unlike readings where poor/needy pair with each other, here neediness stands alone before God's hearing. On the inner-being lens, God is the arena: the destitute condition is precisely what God attends to and refuses to despise.
narratives.story: The poet declares that God listens to the needy and never looks down on his own people, even when they are prisoners. Neediness here is defined by that very relationship: the needy are the ones God hears and does not despise. Their poverty is not paired with anything else in this line - it simply stands before God, and God bends to listen. Even captivity does not make them beneath his notice. This becomes solid ground for hope: whatever the affliction, the destitute are heard.
narratives.variation_note: First of eight readings of H0034:needy (ebyon). Here (Ps 69:33) the needy are the HEARD ones ('the LORD hears the needy and does not despise his own people who are prisoners'); a source-relation is present ('whom the LORD hears and does not despise') and locus (116) is external:god. Across the eight, needy appears as: heard (#1), pleading (#2 Ps 70:5), to-be-delivered-from-the-wicked (#3 Ps 82:4), casting-self-on-God (#4 Ps 86:1), raised/exalted (#5 Ps 107:41), pursued by enemy (#6 Ps 109:16), pleading before God (#7 Ps 109:22), lifted from the ash heap (#8 Ps 113:7). This reading's distinctive is the assurance that God hears and never scorns his captive people - the ground of hope for all the afflicted.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'needy (ebyon - poor and needy)'; type (102) 'status', role (115) characteristic, locus (116) internal:ib-state. The bearer (105) is 'the psalmist'. A SOURCE (103) is present (span-pair): the needy one is he 'whom God his help and deliverer must hasten to save' - grounding the neediness in God's role as help/deliverer. The operation (106) is 'be needy' (inferred). The manner (108) is present and specified: 'pleading God's haste' - the mode of the neediness is urgent entreaty. The coupling (112, span-pair) binds it to 'being poor' - needy and poor twinned. The movement: the destitute self (bearer) -> owns its neediness (operation) -> urgently pleads God, its only help, to hurry (manner) -> paired with poverty (coupling). The discovery (114): the destitution that casts itself wholly on God; the needy psalmist whose only recourse is God his help and deliverer, pleading he not delay - urgency born of utter dependence. Silences: seat (104) 'none'; target (107) 'none' - the neediness aims at no object but its own relief. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) absent: no numeric grading (manner carries the qualitative urgency), no qualifier, no separate effect beyond the hoped-for rescue, no prohibition. On the inner-being lens, God is the arena and the sole recourse: neediness here is not passive but a driving, hastening cry - the interior so empty it can only beg God to run.
narratives.story: The poet ends with a raw, urgent cry: 'I am poor and needy - hurry to me, God! Don't delay!' His neediness here is not quiet resignation but pressing entreaty; it drives him to beg God to move fast. God is named as his only help and rescuer - there is nowhere else to turn. The need is bound up with his poverty, two words for the same emptiness. This is dependence stripped bare: so empty of resources that all he can do is plead for God to come quickly.
narratives.variation_note: Second of eight readings of H0034:needy (ebyon). Here (Ps 70:5) neediness drives an URGENT PLEA - manner is 'pleading God's haste', source-relation is 'whom God his help and deliverer must hasten to save', and it pairs with being poor. It differs from #1 (heard/assured), #3 (deliver from the wicked), #4 (casting self on God), #5 (raised), #6 (pursued), #7 (pleading before God), #8 (lifted from ash heap). The distinctive here is urgency: 'do not delay' - dependence so total it cannot wait.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'poor / afflicted (ani - but I am poor and needy)'; type (102) 'status', role (115) characteristic, locus (116) internal:ib-state. The bearer (105) is 'the psalmist'. The operation (106) is 'be poor / afflicted' (inferred) - a condition owned, not an act. The coupling (112, span-pair) binds it to 'being needy' - poor twinned with needy in the same breath. The movement: the afflicted self (bearer) -> owns poverty (operation) -> paired with neediness (coupling), grounding the plea for God's haste. The discovery (114): the lowly self-estimate that grounds the plea; ani here the psalmist's affliction and poverty, the very estate God is quick to hear - weakness owned as the ground of urgent appeal. Silences: seat (104) 'none'; target (107) 'none' - the poverty aims at no object; manner (108) 'none' - unlike the paired 'needy' reading (which carries 'pleading God's haste'), this poor-row leaves manner unspecified, letting the twin reading carry the urgency. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) absent: no cause of poverty traced, no grading, no qualifier, no separate effect, no prohibition. The distinction from its twin (needy, #2 at same verse) is a finding: 'poor' supplies the bare owned condition, 'needy' supplies the urgent manner - together they build the doubled cry. On the inner-being lens, God is the arena the poor self appeals to; lowliness is here confessed as the very ground of the appeal.
narratives.story: The poet calls himself poor and afflicted - a plain, honest admission of how little he has. This lowly self-estimate is what gives his prayer its force: because he is empty-handed, he throws himself on God. The word sits right beside 'needy', the two together painting a picture of total dependence. This line simply owns the poverty; its twin word carries the urgency of the plea. Weakness, honestly confessed, becomes the very reason he dares to ask.
narratives.variation_note: One of six readings of H6041:poor (ani). Here (Ps 70:5) poverty is the lowly SELF-ESTIMATE that grounds an urgent plea, paired with being needy. It differs from #1 (Ps 40:17, confident lowliness), #3 (Ps 74:21, poor whose rescue turns to praise), #4 (Ps 86:1, poverty as claim on God), #5 (Ps 109:16, poor pursued by enemy), #6 (Ps 109:22, poor pleading against foes). Alongside the needy reading in the same verse, this reading shows 'poor and needy' as a doubled self-description of total dependence.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'poor / afflicted (ani - let the poor and needy praise your name)'; type (102) 'status', role (115) characteristic, locus (116) internal:ib-state. The bearer (105) is 'the poor and needy'. The operation (106) is 'praise God's name' (span-event) - here the lowly are the subject of an active, upward movement, praise. The coupling (112, span-pair) binds them to 'the downtrodden' and notes it 'issues in praise'. The movement: the afflicted (bearer) -> rescued (implied) -> praise God's name (operation) -> joined to the downtrodden, the whole ending in worship (coupling). The discovery (114): the afflicted whose deliverance would turn to praise; the psalmist prays God's rescue may put praise in their mouths instead of shame - the goal of the lament is worship restored. Silences: seat (104) 'none'; target (107) 'none' - though the praise is Godward, the row leaves target unfilled, the operation itself carrying the direction; manner (108) 'none'. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) absent: no cause of poverty, no grading, no qualifier, no separately-named effect beyond the praise, no prohibition. On the inner-being lens, God is the arena the poor turn toward - not in mere plea but in hoped-for praise. This reading is distinctive in the family for making lowliness the seedbed of worship: the desired end of the afflicted's rescue is a mouth filled with praise rather than shame.
narratives.story: In this national lament, the poet prays that God will rescue the poor and afflicted so they can praise his name instead of slinking away in shame. Here the lowly are pictured not just crying out but lifting their voices in worship once help comes. Their poverty is bound up with the whole downtrodden community, and the hoped-for end of it all is praise. The poem does not dwell on how they became poor or how deep it runs; it fixes on the goal - that rescue would turn their humiliation into thanksgiving. The lament reaches for worship restored.
narratives.variation_note: One of six readings of H6041:poor (ani). Here (Ps 74:21) the poor are those whose deliverance should issue in PRAISE ('let the poor and needy praise your name'); the operation is 'praise God's name' and it pairs with the downtrodden. It differs from #1 (confident lowliness), #2 (grounding an urgent plea), #4 (poverty as claim), #5 (pursued by enemy), #6 (pleading against foes). The distinctive: here poverty is oriented toward worship restored - the lament's goal is that the afflicted praise instead of turning back in shame.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'humble / afflicted (anav - all the humble of the earth)'; type (102) 'status', role (115) characteristic; locus (116) external:person - the humble viewed as a class of oppressed people across the earth, not the speaker's inner state. The bearer (105) is 'the humble / oppressed of the earth'. The operation (106) is 'be saved (by God)' (span-event) - God's saving act upon them. The coupling (112, span-pair) makes them 'the object of God's saving judgment'. The movement: the oppressed lowly (bearer) -> God arises to judgment (operation) -> they are saved -> bound as the object of that saving judgment (coupling), while the proud are cut off. The discovery (114): the afflicted, the lowly oppressed; anav here the meek whose vindication is the very aim of God's rising - the humble are saved where the proud princes are cut off (v12). Silences: seat (104) 'none'; target (107) 'none' - the salvation has no further object beyond the humble themselves; manner (108) 'none'. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) absent: no origin of their humility traced, no grading, no qualifier, no separate effect beyond salvation, no prohibition. On the inner-being lens, God is the arena and agent: the humble's lowliness is the condition God's judgment rescues, set in deliberate contrast (directive 5) to the princes whose spirit God cuts off - the same divine act that saves the low destroys the high.
narratives.story: When God rises to judge the earth, the poet says, his aim is to save all the humble - the lowly and oppressed everywhere. Their humility is the very condition his rescue reaches for. And this happens in the same breath as the proud being brought down: God cuts off the spirit of arrogant rulers even as he saves the low. So one act of judgment does two things at once - it lifts the humble and topples the proud. The poem does not explain how these people became humble; it simply names them as the ones God's justice is coming to rescue.
narratives.variation_note: One of five readings of H6035:humbl (anav). Here (Ps 76:9) the humble are the OBJECT SAVED in God's judgment ('to save all the humble of the earth'); the operation is 'be saved (by God)' and locus (116) is external:person. It differs from #1 (led/taught), #2 (see and be glad), #4 (lifted up), #5 (adorned). Distinctive: the humble are vindicated by God's rising judgment precisely where the proud princes are cut off (v12) - lowliness saved as pride is destroyed (directive 5).

narratives.narrative: This reading is a REFUSAL - the dark inverse of humility (directive 5, 6: the failed/dark movement read at full weight). The sense (101) is 'submit / be willing (abah, failed)'; type (102) 'disposition' - a settled bent of the will; role (115) characteristic; locus (116) external:god (the refusal is oriented against God). The bearer (105) is 'Israel'. The operation (106) is 'refuse to submit' - the will actively declining. The target (107) is present: 'to God' - the submission that is withheld is submission toward God. The coupling (112) binds it to 'the failed listening' ('my people did not listen to my voice; Israel would not submit'). The movement: Israel (bearer) -> refuses to submit / be willing (operation) -> toward God (target) -> paired with their deaf non-listening (coupling), issuing (in v12) in God giving them over to their stubborn hearts. The discovery (114): the unwilling heart, obedience declined. Silences: seat (104) 'none'; manner (108) 'none'. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) absent (present:false) - though v12's 'gave them over to their stubborn hearts' is a real consequence, this row does not encode it as a separate effect. That absent effect is worth marking: the passage lets the refusal stand as the disposition itself, its judgment narrated in the next verse rather than tagged here. On the inner-being lens, God is the arena the will sets itself against: this is humility's negation - not lowliness that receives guidance (cf Ps 25:9) but a will that will not bend, and is abandoned to its own stubbornness. Read without valence bias, it is as much a finding about the inner being as any submission: the interior can refuse, and be given over to the refusal.
narratives.story: This is humility turned inside out. God recalls that his people would not bend to him - they refused to submit. It was a set disposition of the will, not a slip: they would not listen and they would not yield. The refusal was aimed squarely at God himself. And the result, spelled out next, is chilling: God simply hands them over to their own stubborn hearts, letting them follow their own counsel. Here we see the inner being's power to say no - a will that will not bow, and is left to the hardness it chose.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'destitute (rush)'; type (102) 'status', role (115) characteristic, locus (116) internal:ib-state. The bearer (105) is 'the destitute'. The operation (106) is 'be left in want' - a passive condition of deprivation. The target (107) is present: 'by the court' - the destitution is framed as what the unjust divine court fails to remedy (the addressees judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked). The coupling (112) pairs the destitute 'with the afflicted' (v3: 'the afflicted and the destitute'). The movement: the utterly poor (bearer) -> left in want (operation) -> by the failing court (target) -> paired with the afflicted (coupling), their want a standing cry against corrupt power. The discovery (114): the utterly poor, whose want cries against corrupt power. Silences: seat (104) 'none'; manner (108) 'none'. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) absent: the origin of the destitution is not traced, no grading, no qualifier, no separately-named effect, no prohibition. On the inner-being lens, the arena is the divine council/court that ought to defend the destitute but does not: destitution here is the lowest social-material estate, and the passage's charge is that just judgment is owed precisely to this condition. The reading anchors the family's 'poor' cluster at its extreme - not merely poor but stripped bare - and turns it into an indictment of unjust power that will not maintain the destitute's right.
narratives.story: In this courtroom scene among the powers of heaven, God demands justice for the utterly destitute - people stripped bare, with nothing. Their condition is one of sheer want, and the charge is that the very authorities meant to defend them have failed, siding with the wicked instead. The destitute stand beside the afflicted, and their empty hands are a silent accusation against corrupt power. The poem does not say how they fell so low; it simply insists that maintaining their right is exactly the duty being neglected. Here lowliness is at its rawest - and it becomes a demand for justice.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'needy (ebyon)'; type (102) 'status', role (115) characteristic, locus (116) internal:ib-state. The bearer (105) is 'the needy'. The operation (106) is 'need deliverance' - the condition of requiring rescue. The target (107) is present: 'from the wicked's hand' - the neediness is defined by the oppressor it must be freed from. The coupling (112) pairs the needy 'with the weak' (v4: 'the weak and the needy'). The movement: the destitute (bearer) -> need deliverance (operation) -> from the wicked's grip (target) -> joined to the weak (coupling), the rescue being the judges' abandoned duty. The discovery (114): the destitute whose deliverance is the judges' abandoned duty. Silences: seat (104) 'none'; manner (108) 'none'. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) absent: no cause of neediness traced, no grading, no qualifier, no separate effect beyond deliverance, no prohibition. On the inner-being lens, the arena is the divine council charged to rescue: neediness here is the estate that has a claim on justice, and the passage's weight is that this claim is being neglected. Paired in the same passage with the destitute (H7326, v3), this reading shows the family's poverty-cluster functioning as the ground of a justice-demand: the low are owed rescue from the powerful.
narratives.story: God commands the powers of heaven to rescue the weak and needy and to snatch them out of the grip of the wicked. Here neediness is a condition that cries out for rescue - people at the mercy of stronger, crueller hands. Their need stands right beside weakness, and freeing them is precisely the duty the corrupt judges have abandoned. The poem does not explain how they became needy; it simply insists they have a claim on justice. Their very helplessness is what should have moved those in power to act.
narratives.variation_note: Third of eight readings of H0034:needy (ebyon). Here (Ps 82:4) the needy are those to be DELIVERED FROM THE WICKED'S HAND ('rescue the weak and the needy; deliver them from the hand of the wicked'); operation 'need deliverance', target 'from the wicked's hand', paired with the weak. It differs from #1 (heard), #2 (urgent plea), #4 (casting self on God), #5 (raised), #6 (pursued), #7 (pleading), #8 (lifted). Distinctive: neediness as the object of a rescue-duty owed by the (failing) divine judges - a social-justice framing.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'needy (ebyon)'; type (102) 'status', role (115) characteristic, locus (116) internal:ib-state. The bearer (105) is 'the psalmist'. The operation (106) is 'be needy' - the owned condition. The target (107) is present: 'before God' - the neediness is presented Godward, as the ground of the appeal. The coupling (112) pairs it 'with being poor' (v1: 'poor and needy'). The movement: the destitute self (bearer) -> owns its neediness (operation) -> lays it before God (target) -> twinned with poverty (coupling), grounding the plea to be heard. The discovery (114): the destitution that casts him wholly on God. Silences: seat (104) 'none'; manner (108) 'none'. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) absent: no origin traced, no grading, no qualifier, no separate effect, no prohibition. On the inner-being lens, God is the arena the needy self turns to and leans on. Held beside its twin 'poor' (H6041, same verse) this reading shows the doubled self-description again: neediness and poverty together are pleaded not as shame but as claim - the very emptiness is offered to God as the reason he should attend.
narratives.story: David begins by telling God plainly: 'I am poor and needy' - and makes that his reason for asking God to listen. Here neediness is owned openly and laid right before God, not hidden. It sits paired with his poverty, two words for the same emptiness, and together they become his claim on God's attention. He is not ashamed of his lack; he presents it as the ground of his appeal. The very fact that he has nothing is why he throws himself entirely on God.
narratives.variation_note: Fourth of eight readings of H0034:needy (ebyon). Here (Ps 86:1) neediness is the ground on which the psalmist CASTS HIMSELF ON GOD ('for I am poor and needy'), target 'before God', paired with being poor. It differs from #1 (heard), #2 (urgent haste), #3 (deliver from the wicked), #5 (raised), #6 (pursued), #7 (pleading against foes), #8 (lifted). Distinctive: neediness as personal claim - David pleads his own destitution as the reason God should incline and hear.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'poor (ani)'; type (102) 'status', role (115) characteristic, locus (116) internal:ib-state. The bearer (105) is 'the psalmist'. The operation (106) is 'be poor / afflicted' - the owned condition. The target (107) is present: 'before God' - the poverty is set Godward as the reason for the plea. The coupling (112) pairs it 'with being needy'. The movement: the afflicted self (bearer) -> owns its poverty (operation) -> presents it to God (target) -> twinned with neediness (coupling), as the ground of the appeal to be answered. The discovery (114): the lowly estate David pleads as his claim on God, humility the ground of the appeal. Silences: seat (104) 'none'; manner (108) 'none'. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) absent: no cause traced, no grading, no qualifier, no separate effect, no prohibition. On the inner-being lens, God is the arena the poor self appeals to; the finding is that lowliness is not a barrier but a basis - the interior's owned poverty is the leverage of the prayer. Paired with its twin 'needy' (H0034, same verse), the doubled confession makes weakness the argument for grace.
narratives.story: David asks God to answer him, and his reason is startling: 'because I am poor and needy.' Here his lowliness is not something to overcome but the very argument of the prayer - he leans on his emptiness as his claim. The poverty stands paired with his need, two sides of the same weakness laid before God. He offers no other credential; his low estate is his case. In God's economy, having nothing turns out to be exactly the ground on which to ask.
narratives.variation_note: One of six readings of H6041:poor (ani). Here (Ps 86:1) poverty is pleaded as a CLAIM ON GOD ('answer me, for I am poor and needy'), target 'before God', paired with being needy. It differs from #1 (confident lowliness), #2 (grounding urgent plea), #3 (poor turning to praise), #5 (pursued by enemy), #6 (pleading against foes). Distinctive: humility as the explicit ground of the appeal - the low estate is itself the argument.

narratives.narrative: This is the family's darkest reading - helplessness with NO resolution (Ps 88 ends without light). The sense (101) is 'helpless (pun)'; type (102) 'state', role (115) characteristic, locus (116) internal:ib-state. The bearer (105) is 'the psalmist'. The operation (106) is 'be helpless / distracted' - a paralysis of the terrified. The target (107) is present: 'under terror' - the helplessness is suffered beneath dread. The coupling (112) pairs it 'with the suffering'. The movement: the afflicted self (bearer) -> undone, paralysed (operation) -> under terror (target) -> bound to his lifelong suffering (coupling), with no rescue named in the passage. The discovery (114): the paralysis of the terrified, undone and without recourse. Silences - and here they matter most (directive 2, 6): seat (104) 'none'; manner (108) 'none'; source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent. The absent EFFECT is the sharpest silence in the whole family: every other lowly-condition reading eventually couples to God's hearing, saving, lifting, or nearness - here there is none. No deliverance-effect is recorded because the psalm grants none; the helplessness simply stands, terror-bound, unrelieved. Read without valence bias (directive 5) and refusing to filter the uncomfortable (directive 6), this is lowliness as sheer collapse before God who feels absent - the inner being at the end of its resources with no answering movement. God is still the arena (the psalmist cries to him, vv13-14), but the passage withholds the rescue the rest of the family enjoys; that withholding is the finding.
narratives.story: This is the bleakest voice in the collection. The poet says he is helpless - undone, paralysed by terror, at the very end of himself. Unlike almost every other cry of the lowly, no rescue follows: there is no lifting, no nearness, no answer recorded here. His helplessness simply stands, wrapped in dread and lifelong suffering. He still cries out to God, but the light does not come in these lines. It is an honest picture of collapse - a person emptied of every resource, with no relief in sight.

narratives.narrative: This reading is humbling as HOSTILE ACT (anah in the piel of oppression) - a rare inversion in the family where 'humble' is what the wicked try to DO to the king, not a virtue. The sense (101) is 'humble / afflict (anah)'; type (102) 'action', role (115) characteristic, locus (116) external:god (the arena is God's covenant protection). The bearer (105) is 'the wicked'. The operation (106) is 'seek to humble' - an aggressive attempt to abase. The target (107) is present: 'the king' - the anointed is the object the wicked would humble. The coupling (112) pairs it 'with the enemy's scheming'. The movement: the wicked (bearer) -> seek to humble/afflict (operation) -> the king (target) -> paired with their scheming (coupling) - but the verse negates it: 'the wicked shall not humble him', God's covenant thwarting the attempt. The discovery (114): the wicked's oppression of the anointed, thwarted by God's covenant. Silences: seat (104) 'none'; manner (108) 'none'; source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) absent - and the absent effect is significant: the humbling does NOT land, so no effect is recorded; God's protection cancels it. On the inner-being lens (directive 5, no valence bias), this reading shows humiliation from the aggressor's side - the will to abase another - held up beside the family's many readings where lowliness is received or God-given. Here it is a weapon aimed at the king and blocked. It preserves an important distinction (directive 8): 'to humble' can be an act of malice, not only a state of virtue; the difference is the whole finding.
narratives.story: Here the word 'humble' flips to its harsh side: it is what the wicked try to do to God's chosen king - to beat him down and abase him. Their aim is oppression, driven by scheming enmity. But the poem immediately blocks it: the wicked will not succeed in humbling him, because God's covenant guards him. So the attempt is real but defeated; the intended humiliation never lands. This shows the darker face of the word - not a lowly heart to be cherished, but a blow aimed at another and turned aside.

narratives.narrative: This reading grounds humility in CREATURELINESS/MORTALITY - man returned to dust at God's word. The sense (101) is 'return to dust (dakka)'; type (102) 'state', role (115) characteristic, locus (116) internal:ib-state. The bearer (105) is 'man / mankind' - the whole race, not an individual sufferer. The operation (106) is 'be turned back to dust' - the reduction of the creature. The target (107) is present: 'by God' - it is God who turns man back. The coupling (112) pairs it 'with God's word "Return"' (v3: 'you return man to dust and say, Return'). The movement: mankind (bearer) -> turned back to dust (operation) -> by God (target/agent) -> triggered by God's word of command (coupling). The discovery (114): the creatureliness and mortality of man, dust to which he is turned back at God's word. Silences: seat (104) 'none'; manner (108) 'none'; source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) absent - no separate effect beyond the return to dust, no grading, no qualifier. On the inner-being lens, God is the arena and agent; this reading is distinctive in the family for locating lowliness not in affliction or penitence but in ontology - the human being IS dust, humbled by mortality itself. It is the metaphysical floor beneath all the other 'poor/needy/humble' readings: the creature's smallness before the eternal God (the psalm's frame, vv1-6). Uncomfortable but supported (directive 6): humility here is simply the truth of what a human is - dust that God speaks back to the ground.
narratives.story: This poem finds humility in the plainest fact of all: human beings are dust, and God turns them back to it with a single word - 'Return.' Here lowliness is not about suffering or repentance but about what a person simply is - a fragile creature before an eternal God. Mankind as a whole is in view, and it is God himself who reduces us again to the ground. There is no drama of rescue here, just the quiet, sobering truth of our mortality. Beneath every other picture of the lowly lies this one: we are small, and we return to dust at God's command.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'destitute (arar)'; type (102) 'status', role (115) characteristic. The bearer (105) is 'the destitute'. The operation (106) is 'be stripped bare' - reduced to nothing. The target (107) is present: 'yet heard by God' - the destitution is met by God's regard. In this row the coupling (112) and locus (116) values appear transposed with their labels (coupling holds 'internal:ib-state', locus holds 'paired with their prayer regarded'); read faithfully, the reading places the destitute WITHIN the inner being as a state and PAIRS the destitution with 'their prayer regarded' - God attends the prayer of the stripped-bare. The movement: the utterly poor (bearer) -> stripped bare (operation) -> yet heard, their prayer regarded (target/coupling). The discovery (114): the utterly poor, whose very destitution God honours with regard ('He regards the prayer of the destitute'). Silences: seat (104) 'none'; manner (108) 'none'; source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) absent - no cause of destitution traced, no grading, no qualifier, no separate effect beyond God's regard. On the inner-being lens, God is the arena: the striking finding is that destitution is not a disqualifier but the very estate God honours with attention - he does not despise their prayer. This joins the family's recurring reversal: the lowest are the ones God stoops to hear.
narratives.story: The poet says that God pays attention to the prayer of the destitute - people stripped of everything - and does not brush their pleading aside. Here being destitute is a bare, emptied condition, yet it is precisely the condition God regards. Their poverty does not shut the door; it is bound up with a prayer that God actually honours. The poem does not explain how they came to have nothing; it simply marvels that God stoops to hear such people. Once again the lowest are the ones God turns toward.

narratives.narrative: This reading is FORCED humiliation as judgment - Israel brought low under enemies. The sense (101) is 'subjection (kana)'; type (102) 'state', role (115) characteristic. The bearer (105) is 'the fathers' (Israel's ancestors). The operation (106) is 'be brought into subjection' - abasement imposed. The target (107) is present: 'under the enemies' power'. In this row coupling (112) and locus (116) values appear transposed with their labels (coupling holds 'internal:ib-state', locus holds 'paired with the oppression'); read faithfully, the subjection is placed WITHIN the inner being as a state and PAIRED with 'the oppression' the enemies inflict. The movement: the fathers (bearer) -> brought into subjection (operation) -> under enemy power (target) -> bound to their oppression (coupling), as the fruit of their rebellion (the psalm's cycle). The discovery (114): the humbling of Israel, abased beneath their foes. Silences: seat (104) 'none'; manner (108) 'none'; source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) absent - no separate effect encoded here, though the wider psalm frames it as chastisement leading to God's remembering (v45). On the inner-being lens, the arena is the foreign oppressor God permits; humility here is not virtue nor mortality but imposed subjugation - the nation crushed low. Read without valence bias (directive 5), this is lowliness as historical judgment: Israel, humbled under its enemies, is nonetheless the object God later regards in his covenant mercy.
narratives.story: Recounting Israel's history, the poet says the ancestors were brought low - forced into submission under their enemies, crushed beneath foreign power. Here being humbled is not a chosen virtue but an imposed defeat, the bitter result of their repeated rebellion. Their subjection is bound up with real oppression at their enemies' hands. Yet the wider poem remembers that even this low point was not the end - God still turned back to them in mercy. It is a sobering picture: a whole people humbled by hard judgment.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'needy (ebyon)'; type (102) 'status', role (115) characteristic. The bearer (105) is 'the needy'. The operation (106) is 'be raised' - God's upward act. The target (107) is present: 'out of affliction' - the needy are raised up from their low estate. In this row coupling (112) and locus (116) values appear transposed with their labels (coupling holds 'internal:ib-state', locus holds 'paired with affliction'); read faithfully, the neediness is a state WITHIN the inner being and is PAIRED with 'affliction' - the very affliction out of which God raises them. The movement: the destitute (bearer) -> raised up (operation) -> out of affliction (target) -> bound to that affliction reversed (coupling). The discovery (114): the poor God exalts, the great reversal of the coda. Silences: seat (104) 'none'; manner (108) 'none'; source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) absent - no cause traced, no grading, no qualifier, no separate effect beyond the raising. On the inner-being lens, God is the arena and agent: the needy's low estate is precisely what God overturns, lifting them and making their families like flocks. This reading exemplifies the family's brightest pattern (set against Ps 88's darkness): lowliness is the launching point of God's upward reversal.
narratives.story: In this psalm's triumphant closing, the poet celebrates how God lifts the needy up out of their misery. Here their neediness is a low, afflicted state - and it is exactly what God reverses, raising them high and letting their families flourish like flocks. Their affliction is not the end of the story; it is the very thing God overturns. This is the bright opposite of despair: the poor lifted, the humble exalted. It is one of the collection's clearest pictures of God turning the lowest into the blessed.
narratives.variation_note: Fifth of eight readings of H0034:needy (ebyon). Here (Ps 107:41) the needy are RAISED/EXALTED ('he raises up the needy out of affliction'), operation 'be raised', target 'out of affliction'. It differs from #1 (heard), #2 (urgent plea), #3 (deliver from wicked), #4 (casting self on God), #6 (pursued), #7 (pleading), #8 (lifted from ash heap). Distinctive: this is the great REVERSAL of the psalm's coda - the poor exalted, families multiplied - lowliness lifted high.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'needy (ebyon)'; type (102) 'status', role (115) characteristic. The bearer (105) is 'the needy'. The operation (106) is 'be pursued' - the needy hunted.
